title: Researching and writing the New Orleans, Oliver and Armstrong chapters of Jazzmen
summary: How Russell, Steve Smith and Lee Smith split the research, advances of about $30 each, Russell's Chicago interviews for the King Oliver chapter and his writing of the Armstrong chapter.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, there's a chapter in Jasmine called New Orleans Music. Yeah. Which you did with Stephen Smith. I think you did that. Now, how did you and he decide to do it together? And how did your research? I don't know who suggested that we do it together.

Steve is much interested in New Orleans Music too, of course. We were partners in the Hot Record Exchange. So, actually at that time he got the idea of opening a store then, a retail store, which didn't open until 1939. Right. But he was very busy organizing things. And actually didn't have time really to work on that chapter except his wife did most of the work and she did a lot of the research. Steve and she would go around and interview people. I'd made a couple of trips to Chicago. We even got an advance. I think that Ramsey got about a, oh, it was roughly a $200 advance from Harcourt. And there were about eight people. So I think we each got a $30 advance royalty deal out of it. So, I made one trip to Chicago. And Ramsey gave me some or maybe all of his money to go there and do research on King Oliver too. He had to do the King Oliver chapter.
So you researched the King Oliver chapter?

Partly. I wouldn't say that. Just the people in Chicago. Right. Because after all, Oliver did most of his important recording and you might say later playing in Chicago. So a lot of people there knew him and several members of the band were still living like, of course, Lil and Louie. And Bill Johnson, Dodds, both the Dodds brothers. So Ramsey couldn't get away from his job at Harcourt. So I did that work for him. All that we could. Unfortunately, no tape machines then. Just had to do it longhand. And I'd take the notes back to New York and try to enlarge a little bit on them. And Steve Smith's wife would type it out. She was a good secretary, as I mentioned before. And would type out the notes then for us. And she and Steve interviewed people in New York, such as Zutty Singleton and Sidney Bechet and a few others from New Orleans were there. So, but when it got time to really write out the stuff, Steve was too busy. So I just took all the notes and material and did the actual writing of it. But I'm not trying to say that Steve really fell down on the job because he was busy with those other things which had to be done then. So then I also wrote the Louis Armstrong chapter.
Was Steve Smith's wife really interested and involved in things?

Well yeah, she was much interested in jazz too. She liked it. What was her name? Lee Smith. Lee Smith. L-E-E. Strange name in a way for a girl. But I guess I know it was Lee Wiley and other people named that I can think of.
